Keystone hardware wallet breach: an attacker stole the device verification key, so fakes could pass its authenticity check. Keystone will destroy 18,835 unsold devices. Got one after Oct 20? Verify with support before use.

#DataBreach #CyberSecurity
items.ig_caption:
18,835 unsold hardware wallets will be destroyed. 🔑

What Keystone disclosed (via The Hacker News, 27 Oct):
→ An attacker got into Keystone's website through a flaw in a third-party data monitoring tool
→ They stole the device verification key: with it, counterfeit devices could pass Keystone's online authenticity check
→ Keystone will destroy 18,835 unsold devices carrying the old key. Devices already sold can't be re-keyed
→ 25,964 buyer records (names, contact details, shipping addresses, orders) were also taken. Recovery phrases, private keys and card details were not involved
→ Keystone says it has seen no counterfeit devices or thefts

What to do: if your Keystone arrived after 20 Oct, don't use it until Keystone support confirms it's genuine. Keystone won't ask you to return a device, so treat recall or refund messages as scams, and never type a recovery phrase into a device you didn't order.

cover.hook: OpenAI's new budget model meets its 'Critical' cyber threshold.
cover.sub: GPT-6.1 Terra costs 50% less than GPT-5.6 Terra and keeps the safeguards built for GPT-6 Astra.

slides.title: What 'Critical' means
slides.body: It's the higher of two cyber thresholds in OpenAI's Preparedness Framework: with tools, a model can find and build working zero-day exploits across many hardened systems with no human involvement, or run a new end-to-end attack from a high-level goal.

slides.label: cheaper than GPT-5.6 Terra
slides.note: API: $1 per million input tokens, $5 per million output

slides.title: The second at this level
slides.body: GPT-6 Astra became OpenAI's first Critical-level cyber model on September 1. Terra keeps Astra's protections, and OpenAI says it held up well in prompt injection tests.

slides.title: Where it runs
slides.body: ChatGPT Work and Codex for Plus, Pro, Enterprise and Edu users, plus the API as gpt-6.1-terra. OpenAI says it completes tasks more than 3x faster than GPT-6 Astra.

slides.title: What to do this week
items: Treat agent tool access as privileged access
Log what your AI agents run, and where
Review your AI policy for security testing
Shorten patch times for internet-facing systems

cover.hook: Ukraine warns: Dahua cameras hijacked through their remote-viewing service.
cover.sub: CERT-UA says attackers watch video, change settings and add accounts, even on cameras not directly online.

slides.title: The way in
slides.body: Dahua's Easy4IP P2P serial numbers are predictable and could be brute-forced at scale without rate limits or lockouts. So cameras with P2P enabled are at risk even when they aren't exposed to the internet.

slides.title: Then the login
slides.body: Weak or known passwords, plus authentication-bypass flaws CVE-2021-33044 and CVE-2021-33045 in outdated firmware. Once in, attackers can view streams, change configuration and create accounts.

slides.label: Dahua cameras hit in an earlier campaign
slides.note: Hunt.io's Operation CameraSwarm, June 17 to July 22, 2026

slides.title: Who's behind it
slides.body: CERT-UA didn't attribute it. Separately, Dutch intelligence (AIVD) warned in July that Russian state actors compromise IP cameras across the EU, NATO states and Ukraine for espionage.

slides.title: Check your cameras
items: Turn off P2P if you don't need it
Keep cameras off the open internet
Hunt for unknown accounts and logins from 127.0.0.1

items.question: Does anyone on your team actually own the cameras?
items.x_text:
Dahua IP cameras / CVE-2021-33044: CERT-UA warns attackers are hijacking cameras in Ukraine via the Easy4IP P2P service and old auth-bypass flaws, then viewing streams and adding accounts. Disable P2P, update firmware.

#IoTSecurity #CyberSecurity
items.ig_caption:
Your camera doesn't need to be online to be hijacked. 📹

What CERT-UA warned (via The Hacker News, 27 Oct):
→ Attackers are taking over Dahua IP cameras and DVRs in Ukraine: viewing streams, changing settings, creating accounts
→ The main entry point is Easy4IP, Dahua's P2P remote-viewing service, whose serial numbers are predictable
→ Then weak passwords or the old auth-bypass flaws CVE-2021-33044 and CVE-2021-33045 in outdated firmware
→ An earlier campaign tracked by Hunt.io hit 14,530+ Dahua cameras between June and July 2026
→ CERT-UA didn't attribute it; Dutch intelligence warned in July that Russian state actors compromise IP cameras for espionage

What to do: turn off P2P if you don't need it, keep cameras off the internet, update firmware, and look for unknown accounts and DVRIP logins from 127.0.0.1.

items.x_text:
Amadey malware: Australia's Signals Directorate got into an Amadey backend and cut it off from about 180,000 infected computers. Stolen credentials can still be used months later, so reset and revoke sessions.

#Malware #CyberSecurity
items.ig_caption:
180,000 infected computers. Cut off in one move. 🇦🇺

What happened (via The Hacker News, 27 Oct):
→ Australia's Signals Directorate (ASD) got into the backend of an Amadey malware operation
→ It disconnected the controller from about 180,000 infected computers worldwide, some in Australia
→ Amadey has been sold to criminals since 2018; its main job is installing more malware, such as the StealC infostealer
→ ESET has identified 53 separate Amadey botnets, so this is one of many
→ The takedown doesn't undo earlier theft: stolen credentials can sit unused for months

What to do: if a machine was infected, treat its saved passwords and live sessions as stolen. Reset them, revoke sessions and tokens, and watch for logins that skip MFA via stolen cookies.
